title: Magnets and Metal
strapline: The invisible pull — testing, sorting and asking "why?".
intent: Magnets create real, testable wonder — an invisible force children can feel and investigate.
Predicting and testing what a magnet will pick up is early scientific thinking.
Sorting objects into "sticks" and "doesn't stick" builds classification.
Magnets provoke a stream of genuine "why?" and "how?" questions.
Describing what they notice grows precise, curious talk.
implementation: Offer strong, safe magnets and a tray of objects, some magnetic and some not.
Invite predictions first — "do you think this will stick?" — then test.
Sort the objects into two groups and talk about what the "sticky" ones have in common.
Add magnets to water play, sand and a treasure hunt for hidden metal.
Model the vocabulary: attract, pull, metal, magnet — and welcome their questions.
Let children lead investigations and follow their surprises.
key_questions: Do you think the magnet will pick this up? Why?
What is the same about all the things that stick?
What could we use the magnet to find?
Why do you think it won't stick to this one?
What happens when two magnets come close?

impact.text: Children explore forces and materials and how things behave through play.
Children predict and then test what a magnet will pick up.
Children sort and notice what magnetic objects have in common.
Children ask "why" and "how" questions and expect real answers.
Children describe what they observe using new vocabulary.

enhancements: Strong, safe magnets in different shapes (bar, horseshoe, wand).
A sorting tray of magnetic and non-magnetic objects.
A magnetic wand and metal shapes for treasure hunts.
Magnets to explore in water and sand trays.
Recording sheets for "will it stick?" predictions.
Books about magnets and forces to extend the wondering.

playing_exploring: Children investigate the pull of magnets and test objects with real curiosity.
active_learning: Children stick at their investigation and are driven by their own questions.
creating_thinking: Children predict, test and work out what magnetic objects have in common.
